n: Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH) in Metabolism and Clinical Medicine

faq.a: It blocks ALDH, causing acetaldehyde to accumulate after alcohol intake, producing vasodilation and flushing.
Small amounts may be tolerated, but accumulation of acetaldehyde increases cancer risk and can cause severe symptoms.
faq.q: Can a patient with ALDH2 deficiency drink alcohol safely?

faq.a: Fomepizole competitively inhibits ADH, preventing formation of toxic formaldehyde and formic acid.
faq.q: What is the role of fomepizole in methanol poisoning?

exam: A 35‑year‑old man presents after ingesting windshield washer fluid; ABG shows pH 7.05, HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L. What is the next step — Administer fomepizole to block ADH and arrange haemodialysis.
A patient of East African descent reports facial flushing after a glass of beer. Which genetic test explains this — ALDH2*2 polymorphism, indicating reduced ALDH activity.
In a rural clinic without dialysis, how would you manage severe methanol poisoning — Use high‑dose ethanol infusion to compete with methanol for ADH, give folate, and arrange transfer.
Why is measuring serum acetaldehyde not routinely required in acute alcohol intoxication — Levels fluctuate rapidly and clinical signs guide management.
A child with refractory seizures is found to have low pyridoxine; which enzyme defect should be considered — ALDH7A1 deficiency (pyridoxine‑dependent epilepsy).
During disulfiram therapy a patient drinks alcohol and develops severe nausea. What is the pathophysiology — Disulfiram inhibits ALDH, causing acetaldehyde buildup.
Explain why ALDH2 deficiency increases esophageal cancer risk — Accumulated acetaldehyde is a carcinogen that damages esophageal epithelium.
What laboratory finding distinguishes methanol poisoning from diabetic ketoacidosis — High anion‑gap metabolic acidosis with normal/low glucose and elevated serum formic acid.
ai.title: Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH) in Metabolism and Clinical Medicine
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: ALDH enzymes detoxify aldehydes from alcohol, drugs and endogenous metabolism. Deficiency or inhibition can cause toxic accumulation, leading to acute poisoning, chronic liver disease and genetic disorders.

b: Located mainly in mitochondria (ALDH2) and cytosol (ALDH1).
Key for ethanol, methanol, and retinol metabolism.
sections.p: Aldehyde dehydrogenases are a family of NAD⁺‑dependent enzymes that oxidize aldehydes to their corresponding acids, protecting cells from reactive intermediates.

b: Mitochondrial ALDH2 has high affinity for acetaldehyde.
sections.p: Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) converts ethanol → acetaldehyde → (ALDH) → acetate. In methanol poisoning, ADH makes formaldehyde, then ALDH converts it to formic acid, the toxic metabolite.

b: ALDH2*2 allele reduces activity → flushing, increased cancer risk.
Disulfiram blocks ALDH, causing acetaldehyde buildup.
sections.p: ALDH activity is modulated by genetic polymorphisms, substrate availability, and inhibition by drugs (e.g., disulfiram).

b: ALDH2 deficiency → alcohol‑induced flushing, higher esophageal cancer risk.
Methanol poisoning → formic acid accumulation → optic nerve damage.
sections.p: Deficiency or inhibition leads to accumulation of toxic aldehydes, causing metabolic acidosis, neurologic injury, or chronic organ damage.

b: Acute methanol or ethylene glycol ingestion: give fomepizole or ethanol to block ADH, then support ALDH activity.
Disulfiram therapy for alcohol dependence relies on ALDH inhibition.
Screen for ALDH2*2 in East African populations with high alcohol use.
sections.p: Understanding ALDH informs management of acute poisonings, interpretation of alcohol‑related symptoms, and counseling of patients with genetic variants.

t.b: Confirms aldehyde accumulation; high levels suggest ALDH inhibition or deficiency; not routinely available – rely on clinical picture.
Detects metabolic acidosis from formic acid in methanol poisoning; look for low pH, low HCO₃⁻, high anion gap.
Identifies at‑risk individuals; not essential for acute care, useful for counseling.

b: Methanol poisoning: give fomepizole (or ethanol if unavailable) to inhibit ADH, then haemodialysis to remove formic acid.
Alcohol‑induced flushing: advise avoidance; consider riboflavin supplementation to improve residual ALDH activity.
Disulfiram reaction: stop disulfiram, give supportive care, monitor for dehydration.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support detoxification, and monitor for complications.

b: Liver failure: high bilirubin, coagulopathy, not rapid improvement with ADH blockade.
Sepsis: fever, leukocytosis, source infection; aldehyde poisoning lacks infectious signs.
sections.p: ALDH deficiency is sometimes mistaken for liver failure or sepsis because both cause elevated lactate and acidosis.

b: Rely on clinical context rather than a single lab value.
sections.p: Normal serum acetaldehyde does not rule out ALDH deficiency if sampling is delayed; formic acid may be cleared quickly after dialysis.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) after suspected methanol ingestion.
Rapid visual loss or ocular pain in a poisoning scenario.
Unexplained high anion‑gap acidosis with neurologic deterioration.
